Question no. 1. What do you mean by ‘Memorandum of Association?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The term The Memorandum of Association (“MoA”) is a fundamental legal document  
that outlines the company's constitution, objectives, and powers. It serves as the  
company's charter or foundation upon which the company's activities are built. As  
per section 2(56) of the Companies Act, 2013 (“Act”), 2(56) the Memorandum means the  
memorandum of association of a company as originally framed or as altered from time to  
time in pursuance of any previous company law or of this Act.  
Memorandum of Association describes the purpose for which the company is formed.  
It defines the powers of the company and the conditions under which it operates. It is a  
document that contains all the rules and regulations that govern a company’s  
relations with the outside world. It is mandatory for every company to have a  
Memorandum of Association which defines the scope of its operations. Once prepared,  
the company cannot operate beyond the scope of the MoA. If the company goes  
beyond the scope, then the action will be considered ultra vires and hence will be  
void. The MoA is a public document. Section 3 of the Companies Act describes the  
importance of MoA by stating that, for registering a company,  
 For a private company, two or more people are required;  
 For a public company, seven or more people are required;  
 For a one-person company, only one person is required.  
Therefore, in all the above-mentioned cases, the concerned people should first subscribe  
to the MoA before registering the company with Registrar. This emphasizes the  
importance of the MoA for registering a company.  
Section 4(5) of the Companies Act states that a memorandum should be in any Form as  
given in Tables A, B, C, D, and E of Schedule 1. The Tables are of different kinds because  
of different kinds of companies.  
 Table A –applicable to a company limited by shares.  
 Table B –applicable to a company limited by guarantee and not having a share  
capital.  
 Table C –applicable to a company limited by guarantee and having a share capital.  
 Table D –applicable to an unlimited company not having a share capital.  
 Table E –applicable to an unlimited company having a share capital.  
2
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
Section 4 of the Companies Act, 2013 states the contents of the MoA which details all  
the essential information that the MoA should contain.  
 Name Clause: The MoA begins with the name clause, which states the name of  
the company being incorporated. The name stated in the MoA shall not be,  
identical to the name of another company; too nearly resembling the name of an  
already existing company and undesirable name will also not be allowed to be  
chosen and names which in any way indicate that the company is working for the  
government are also not allowed.  



If a company is a public company, then the word 'Limited' should be there  
in the name.  
If a company is a private company, then 'Private Limited' should be there  
in the name.  
The above condition is not applicable to Section 8 companies.  
 Registered Office Clause: This clause specifies the registered office address of  
the company. It includes the state in which the registered office is situated and is  
used for the purpose of all communications with the company. Section 12 of the  
Act provides that before incorporation of the company, it is sufficient to mention  
only the name of the state where the company is located. However, after  
incorporation, the company has to state the exact location of the registered office.  
The company has to within 30 days of its incorporation and at all times, thereafter,  
have a registered office capable of receiving and acknowledging all  
communications and notices as may be addressed to it. It is mandatory for every  
company to fix its name and address of its registered office on the outside of every  
office in which the business of the company takes place. If the company is a one-  
person company, then “One-person Company” should be written in brackets below  
the affixed name of the company.  
 Object Clause: This outlines the purpose for which the company is formed. It  
contains both the main object as well as the ancillary objects for which the  
company is formed. The objects must be well defined and lawful a. It defines the  
scope of activities that the company is authorized to undertake and therefore, any  
activity not mentioned in this clause is considered beyond the company's scope of  
activity and so it is ultra vires and thus, void (Doctrine of Ultra Vires).  
 Liability Clause: This clause defines the liability of members. In a company limited  
by shares, members' liability is limited to the unpaid amount on their shares. In a  
company limited by guarantee, members' liability is limited to a predetermined  
amount they agree to contribute in the event of winding up. Thus, this clause  
provides legal protection to the shareholders by protecting them from being held  
personally liable for the loss of the company.  
 Capital Clause: This clause states the maximum amount of authorized share  
capital the company is authorized to issue or the maximum amount with which the  
company is registered. It also includes details about the number of shares, kinds  
of shares etc., any increase or reduction in share capital requires compliance with  
legal procedures.  
3
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
 Association Clause or the Subscription clasue: The last clause confirms that  
the subscribers to the MoA agree to become members of the company and take  
up shares as specified. Each subscriber's name, address, occupation, and number  
of shares subscribed are mentioned.  
Alteration of MoA: The MoA can be altered after incorporation. Changes to the MoA may  
relate to the name, registered office, objects, liability, capital, or other provisions. The term  
“alteration” is defined in Section 2(3) of the Act, as any additions, omissions or  
substitutions. A company can alter the memorandum only to the extent as permitted by  
the Act. According to Section 13, the company can alter the clauses in the memorandum  
by passing a special resolution.  
Thus, the MoA is a vital legal document that defines the company's scope, purpose, and  
fundamental structure. It serves as a reference point for the company's activities, ensuring  
transparency and accountability to shareholders, regulators, stakeholders, and others.  
NOTE: For details relating to Alteration of MoA refer Section 13 of the Act and the Notes  
provided.

Question no. 2. What do you mean by ‘Articles of Association?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
Articles of Association' under the Companies Act, 2013 (“Act”) refer to a crucial legal  
document that defines the internal rules, regulations, byelaws, and operational framework  
of a company. This document outlines the roles and responsibilities of the company's  
directors, officers, and shareholders in various aspects of the company's functioning. The  
Articles of Association (“AoA”) work in conjunction with the Memorandum of Association  
(MoA) to establish the company's constitution and the manner in which it will operate. The  
4
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
AoA thus, helps in governing the management of internal affairs of the company. AoA has  
been defined under section 2 (5) of the Act as ““articles” means the articles of association  
of a company as originally framed or as altered from time to time or applied in pursuance  
of any previous company law or of this Act”.  
The AoA is a very important document for a company as it holds the rules, regulations and  
byelaws for internal administration and management of the company. It is basically for the  
internal management of the company. In the AoA all the:  
 powers of directors and other officials are described;  
 rights and obligations are prescribed;  
 restrictions are also laid down in case of a private company;  

provisions regarding the shares are also mentioned.  
Thus, AoA regulates the internal management of the company and the relationship of the  
company with its members and officers. Some of the provisions as contained in the AoA  
are:  
 Share Capital: It outlines the classes and types of shares the company can issue,  
the rights associated with each class, value of each share, etc.  
 Alteration of capital  
 Voting rights and proxies  
 Meetings rules and proceedings  
 Directors: Their appointment, remuneration, meetings etc.  
 Accounts and audit: When will be an audit of the accounts will be done  
 Winding up procedure etc.  
So, the AoA is a binding contract between the company and its shareholders, as well as  
among shareholders themselves. It acts as an internal rulebook, guiding the  
company's day-to-day operations and interactions between stakeholders. Any  
provision in the AoA that contradicts the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and/or  
the MoA is deemed void to the extent of the contradiction.  
Further, the 2013 Act brought into effect an important provision relating to the  
Entrenchment of the AoA under section 5. According to this provision the alteration in  
the AoA should be such that the altered provisions become more restrictive than those  
applicable in the case of a special resolution. In other words, it means the inclusion of  
specific provisions in AoA that can only be altered or removed through a more  
rigorous process than usual. The Act allows companies to entrench certain provisions  
in their AoA to provide them with greater protection and stability and thus, safeguard  
specific clauses or rules within the AoA from being altered or removed easily. These  
provisions require a more stringent procedure for amendment than regular  
provisions in the AoA. Entrenchment provision can be introduced in AoA:  
 during formation/incorporation; or  
 amendment in the Article by  

a special resolution- Public Company &  
5
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  

agreement between all the members- private company  
Alteration of AoA: The Act provides companies with the flexibility to alter their AoA to  
adapt to changing circumstances, business needs, and regulatory requirements.  
Alteration of AoA involves making changes to the internal rules and regulations that govern  
the company's operations and management. However, any alteration in the AoA is  
subjected to the provisions of this Act and the conditions contained in the MoA. Section  
14 of the Act provides that the provision for the alteration of the AoA of the company and  
specifies that subject to the provisions of this particular section and the conditions of the  
MoA, a company may alter its AoA through a special resolution and add that any alteration  
made shall be as valid as if it was originally contained in the AoA.  
Thus, the Articles of Association play a critical role in shaping the internal structure and  
functioning of a company. They provide a clear framework for decision-making,  
governance, and interactions within the company, ensuring transparency and  
accountability in its operations.  
NOTE: For details relating to Alteration of AoA refer Section 2(3) and 14 of the Act and  
the Notes provided.

Question no. 3. Write short notes on the Doctrine of Constructive Notice?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
6
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
The 'Doctrine of Constructive Notice' is a legal principle or doctrine that relates to the  
notice given to all persons regarding the contents of Memorandum of Association and  
Articles of Association. When these documents are registered with the Registrar of  
Companies, they are deemed to be public documents and so, every person has  
access to them. Therefore, everyone having access to these public documents can  
inspect these documents and get their copies by paying the requisite fee. It is, therefore,  
assumed that any person who deals with the company is familiar with the contents  
of these documents. This is known as constructive notice.  
Further, according to this doctrine, every person dealing with or proposing to enter into a  
contract with the company is presumed to have constructive notice of the contents of  
these public documents of the company. So, if a person deals with a company in a  
manner which is inconsistent with the provisions contained in these documents, he will not  
acquire any right under the contract against the company.  
For example, if the Articles provides that a bill of exchange must be signed by two  
directors, a person who has a bill signed by only one director cannot claim payment upon  
such bill.  
Therefore, a person dealing with a company is held accountable for having knowledge  
of the provisions contained in the company's public documents. If a provision in the AoA  
or any public document affects a transaction, the parties involved are presumed to be  
aware of it as the ignorance of the provisions of public documents is generally not  
accepted as an excuse for any contractual or legal implications arising from such  
documents.  
Thus, it can be said that if a person enters into a contract with a company and claims  
ignorance of certain provisions of the company's AoA, the doctrine of constructive  
notice may be invoked, and he may be held accountable for having knowledge of  
those provisions since they are part of the public records. Therefore, the 'Doctrine of  
Constructive Notice' holds that persons dealing with a company are presumed to have  
knowledge of its public documents, filed with regulatory authorities thereby ensuring  
transparency and fairness in business transactions.

Question no. 4. Write short notes on the ‘Doctrine of Indoor Management’?  
Ans.  
7
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
.
Introduction:  
The 'Doctrine of Indoor Management' is a legal principle that protects the interests of  
third parties who transact with a company. According to this doctrine, outsiders dealing  
with a company are entitled to assume that the internal procedures and formalities  
required for the company's operations have been properly complied with. This  
doctrine essentially protects third parties from the company's internal irregularities  
or deficiencies. In other words, this doctrine provides that the persons dealing with the  
company are bound to see that the proposed deals are in accordance with the provisions  
of the Memorandum of Association and the Articles of Association of the company. But  
they are not bound to enquire into the internal regularity or procedural compliance of the  
company. If the proposed deal is within the scope of these two documents, the company  
will be bound by the deal and the rights of the dealing parties will not be adversely affected  
in any way by the irregularity of the internal procedures.  
The rule on which the doctrine of Indoor Management is based was laid down in Royal  
British Bank Vs. Turquand. Therefore, this rule is also known as the ‘Turquand rule’.  
Example: The Articles of a bank provided that the directors can borrow by issuing bond  
provided they were authorised by a resolution at the general meeting. The directors of the  
bank issued a bond to Mr. A without being authorised. Held, the Bank was bound by the  
bond and Mr. A was entitled to assume that the necessary resolution had been passed.  
Thus, the doctrine recognizes that an outsider dealing with a company cannot be  
expected to know the company's internal affairs, such as its internal procedures,  
authority of officers, or compliance with internal rules. Therefore, when a third party enters  
into a transaction with a company and relies on the authority of an officer or a document,  
the third party's actions are considered valid even if there are internal irregularities. If an  
officer exceeds their authority or if there are internal defects, outsiders dealing with the  
company are not held responsible for these internal issues.  
However, the doctrine does not protect outsiders if they have actual knowledge of  
any irregularities or lack of authority. If an outsider has reasons to suspect that  
something is wrong with the transaction or that the person, they are dealing with lacks  
authority, they are not protected by the doctrine. So, where a third party dealing with a  
company has actual knowledge or reason to believe that the transaction or the person  
they are dealing with is not in accordance with the company's internal procedures or  
authority in such cases, the third party cannot avail themselves of the protection provided  
by this doctrine. In other words, the protection provided by this doctrine does not extend  
to situations where the third party has actual knowledge of any deficiencies or irregularities  
in the transaction or the authority of the company's officers. So the exceptions to this  
doctrine are having a knowledge of any irregularities, forgery and negligence.  
Example: If a third party is aware that a particular officer has been suspended or removed  
from their position in the company, and yet they enter into a transaction with that officer  
based on their apparent authority. In such a scenario, the third party cannot claim  
protection under the 'Doctrine of Indoor Management' because they have actual  
knowledge of the officer's lack of authority.  
8
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
The exception ensures that the doctrine is not misused by parties who  
have knowledge of irregularities or improper conduct within a company. It  
encourages third parties to exercise reasonable diligence and not to turn a blind eye to  
obvious signs of wrongdoing and so the protection it provides to third parties is not  
absolute. It encourages transparency and responsible conduct among all parties involved  
in business transactions.  
Thus, this legal principle provides a shield to third parties dealing with a company  
from internal irregularities or deficiencies in the company's operations. It ensures  
that outsiders can rely on the apparent authority and representations of the  
company's officers without being held responsible for internal matters beyond their  
knowledge. In other words, the doctrine ensures that third parties who transact with a  
company can rely on the outward appearances and representations made by the  
company's officers without probing into its internal affairs. It maintains the stability and  
predictability of business transactions by providing protection to innocent parties.

Question no. 5. Write short notes on the ‘Doctrine of Ultra Vires’?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The 'Doctrine of Ultra Vires' is a legal principle that relates to the powers and  
limitations of a company as defined in its Memorandum of Association. The term  
"ultra vires" is derived from Latin word “ultra” meaning ‘beyond’ and the word  
‘vires’ meaning powers. Thus, ultra vires means "beyond the powers" of a company.  
This doctrine is essential for ensuring that a company operates within the scope of its  
authorized powers and does not engage in activities that exceed its legal boundaries.  
According to this doctrine a company can only engage in activities that are explicitly stated  
in its Memorandum of Association and so any action taken by the company beyond that  
is considered ultra vires and, therefore, void, and unenforceable. The main objective of  
the doctrine is to protect the interests of shareholders, creditors, and other stakeholders  
by preventing a company from acting beyond its proposed scope.  
As the Memorandum of Association of a company defines its powers so any activity of  
a company beyond its Memorandum is ultra vires the company and such an act is  
9
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
void and cannot be ratified even by unanimous resolution of all the shareholders. The  
doctrine provides clarity and certainty to shareholders, creditors, and other parties  
dealing with the company thereby preventing the company from unexpectedly  
venturing into activities beyond its intended scope, which could lead to financial risks.  
The doctrine provides transparency and accountability in corporate activities.  
The doctrine of ultra-vires first time originated in the classic case of Ashbury Railway  
Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche where it was held that the contract was ultra-vires  
the Memorandum of the company, and, thus, null and void.  
The 'Doctrine of Ultra Vires' ensures that companies operate within their authorized  
powers as defined in their Memorandum of Association. It safeguards the interests of  
stakeholders and maintains transparency and accountability in corporate activities.

Question no. 6. Explain the meaning of ‘lifting of Corporate Veil’ under the Companies Act, 2013.  
What are the circumstances when it can be lifted?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
Under the Companies Act when the company is incorporated, it is accorded the status of  
being a separate legal entity which demarcates the status of the company and the  
members or shareholders that it is composed of. This concept of differentiation is  
called a Corporate Veil. On the other hand, the concept of "lifting of the corporate veil"  
refers to the legal principle where the separation between a company and its  
members is disregarded, revealing the true nature and identity of the individuals who  
are behind the company. In other words, the legal fiction that treats a company as a  
separate legal entity distinct from its members is temporarily set aside to expose the  
individuals who are actually responsible for the acts done on behalf of the company. This  
doctrine is applied in specific situations where the company's separate personality is used  
for fraudulent, unfair, or unlawful purposes.  
10  
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
One of the main characteristic features of a company is that the company is a separate  
legal entity distinct from its members. Lifting the corporate refers to the possibility of  
looking behind the company’s framework or behind the company’s separate personality.  
The circumstances under which corporate veil may be lifted can be categorized  
broadly into two following heads:  
 Statutory provisions: This involves situations where the law itself allows for the  
lifting of the corporate veil. In such cases, the individuals who are actually in control  
of the company's actions can be held accountable, and the law prescribes  
penalties for them, examples: reduction of number of members below the statutory  
minimum, misstatement in the prospectus, failure to refund the application fee,  
ultra vires acts etc.  
 Judicial grounds: The courts can lift the corporate veil on various grounds, such  
as when a company is sham or fraudulent, to avoid welfare legislation, to determine  
the true character of a company, or to protect revenue from tax evasion. The judicial  
grounds are applied based on the specific circumstances of each case, fraud, tax  
evasion, violation of public policy or the public interest etc.  
The concept of "lifting the corporate veil" is a legal principle through which courts can  
unveil the hidden reality behind a company's legal façade. It enables the identification and  
accountability of individuals responsible for wrongful or fraudulent activities carried out  
using the company as a cover. This doctrine is invoked in specific situations where the  
interests of justice, fairness, and public interest demand that the true beneficiaries and  
responsible parties be revealed.

Question no. 7. What is meant by the incorporation of company as per Companies Act 2013  
Explain in detail.  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
11  
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
Incorporation of a company under the Companies Act 2013 refers to the formal legal  
process through which a new business entity is established as a separate legal entity with  
its own distinct identity, rights, and obligations. This process involves various steps and  
requirements that must be fulfilled to give the company legal recognition and standing.  
Under section 3 of the Act the basic requirements of forming a company have been  
detailed like the requirement for the minimum number of members for forming a company  
which lays the foundation for the initiation of incorporation of a company . However,  
section 7 lays down the provisions and procedures for the incorporation of a  
company as under:  
 Filing of company registration papers with the registrar: To incorporate a  
company, the subscriber has to file the following company registration papers with  
the registrar within whose jurisdiction the location of the registered office of the  
proposed company falls.  


MoA & AoA  
Person who is engaged in the formation of the company has to give a  
declaration regarding compliance of all the requirements and rules of the  
Act  

Each subscriber to the Memorandum and individuals named as first  
directors in the Articles should submit an affidavit with details such as:  
o declaration regarding non-conviction of any offence with respect to  
the formation, promotion, or management of any company  
o he has not been found guilty of fraud or any breach of duty to any  
company  
o the documents filed with the registrar are complete and true to the  
best of his knowledge  


Address for correspondence until the registered office is set-up  
If the subscriber to the Memorandum is an individual, then h his full name,  
residential address, and nationality along with a proof of identity. If the  
subscriber is a body corporate, then prescribed documents need to be  
provided.  


Individuals mentioned as subscribers to the Memorandum in the Articles  
need to provide the details specified in the point above along with the  
Director Identification Number.  
The individuals mentioned as first directors of the company in the Articles  
must provide particulars of interests in other firms or bodies corporate along  
with their consent to act as directors of the company.  
 Issuing the Certificate of Incorporation: Once the Registrar receives the  
required documents and information, he registers all information and documents  
and issues a Certificate of Incorporation to the company.  
 Corporate Identity Number: The Registrar also allocates a Corporate Identity  
Number to the company which is a distinct identity for the company. The allotment  
12  
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
of CIN is on and from the company’s incorporation date. The certificate carries this  
date.  
 Maintaining copies of Company registration papers: The company must  
maintain and preserve at its registered office copies of all documents and  
information as originally filed.  
 Furnishing false information at the time of incorporation: If any person  
furnishes any false or incorrect particulars of any information or suppresses any  
material information, of which he is aware in any of the documents filed with the  
Registrar in relation to the registration of a company, he shall be liable for action  
under section 447.  
 The company is already incorporated based on false information: Where, at  
any time after the incorporation of a company, it is proved that the company has  
been got incorporated by furnishing any false or incorrect information or  
representation or by suppressing any material fact or information in any of the  
documents or declaration filed or made for incorporating such company, or by any  
fraudulent action, the promoters , the persons named as the first directors of the  
company and the persons making declaration shall each be liable for action under  
section 447.  
 Order of the National Company Law Tribunal: Where a company has been got  
incorporated by furnishing any false or incorrect information or representation or  
by suppressing any material fact or information in any of the documents or  
declaration filed or made for incorporating such company or by any fraudulent  
action, the Tribunal may, on an application made to it, on being satisfied that the  
situation so warrants:  

pass such orders, as it may think fit, for regulation of the management of  
the company including changes, if any, in its memorandum and articles, in  
public interest or in the interest of the company and its members and  
creditors; or  


direct that liability of the members shall be unlimited; or  
direct removal of the name of the company from the register of companies;  
or  


pass an order for the winding up of the company; or  
pass such other orders as it may deem fit.  
However, before making any order the Tribunal shall:  

give the company a reasonable opportunity of being heard in the matter;  
and  

take into consideration the transactions entered into by the company,  
including the obligations, if any, contracted or payment of any liability.  
Therefore, the incorporation process under the Companies Act involves multiple steps and  
thus, provides the company with a separate legal identity, distinct from its owners, and  
enables it to conduct business activities, enter contracts, and assume legal rights and  
obligations.

Question no. 8. Describe Meaning and characteristics of company as per the Companies Act,  
2013?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The word ‘company’ is derived from the Latin word Com Panis wherein Com means  
‘with or together’ and Panis means ‘bread’. Under the Companies Act, 2013 (“Act”), a  
company is a legal entity formed by a group of individuals to conduct business activities  
with a common objective of earning profits. This Act provides comprehensive guidelines  
and regulations for the incorporation, management, operation, and dissolution of  
companies in India. According to section 2(20) of this Act “company” means a  
company incorporated under this Act or under any previous company law.  
As per the Act, a company is defined as a separate legal entity that is incorporated and  
registered under the provisions of this Act. Being a mere creation of law, it possesses only  
those properties which the charter of its creation confers upon it either expressly or as  
incidental to its very existence. The characteristic features of a company are:  
 Incorporated Entity: A company is created by a process of incorporation, which  
involves registration with the Registrar of Companies. This process grants the  
company a separate legal identity from its members, enabling it to own assets,  
incur liabilities, and enter into contracts in its own name.  
 Separate Legal Entity: The company is considered a separate legal entity distinct  
from its members. It can sue and be sued in its own name, own property, and enter  
into contracts. This legal separation ensures that the company's actions are distinct  
from those of its shareholders. This is one of the outstanding features of a company  
i.e., its independent corporate existence.  
 Perpetual Succession: A company enjoys perpetual succession, meaning its  
existence is not affected by the death, insolvency, or departure of its members.  
The company continues to exist regardless of changes in ownership, allowing for  
long-term stability in business operations.  
14  
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
 Common Seal: A company uses a common seal as an official signature on legal  
documents and contracts. This seal acts as the company's authorized signature  
and confirms the authenticity of documents. However, by an amendment now there  
is no compulsion on the company to have a common seal.  
 Limited Liability: One of the most significant features of a company is limited  
liability. Members liability becomes limited or restricted to the nominal value of the  
shares taken by them in a company limited by shares or the amount guaranteed  
by them in a company limited by guarantee.  
 Transferability of Shares: Section 44 of the Act, declares that “the shares or  
debentures or any other interest of any member in a company shall be a movable  
property that can be transferred in the manner provided in the Article of the  
company.”  
 Capacity to Sue and Be Sued: A company has the legal capacity to initiate legal  
proceedings or be the target of legal actions in its own name. This ability ensures  
that the company can protect its interests and rights legally.  
Theus, a company under the Companies Act is a distinct legal entity characterized by its  
separate legal existence, limited liability for shareholders, perpetual succession, and other  
features that enable it to engage in business activities as an independent entity. These  
characteristics provide a framework for the operation, governance, and management of  
companies in India.

Question no. 9. What is meant by public offer and private placement under the Companies  
Act?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
Under the Companies Act, 2013, the terms "public offer" and "private placement" relate  
to two distinct methods of raising capital by companies. These methods have specific  
regulations and requirements that companies must adhere to. As a business cannot run  
without funding so it chooses to adopt these methods to raise fund as per the  
provisions of the Companies Act (“Act”).  
15  
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
Section 23 of Companies Act, 2013 deals with public offer and private placement.  
 A public company may issue securities:  



to public through prospectus known as "public offer" by complying with the  
provisions of Part I of the Act; or  
through private placement by complying with the provisions of Part II of  
the Act; or  
through a rights issue or a bonus issue. II  
In case of a listed company or a company which intends to get its securities listed also  
must comply with the provisions of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992.  
 A private company may issue securities:  


by way of rights issue or bonus issue; or  
through private placement by complying with the provisions of Part II of  
the Act.  
A public offer is a method by which a company invites the general public to  
subscribe to its shares or debentures. This process involves the issuance of a  
prospectus, which contains detailed information about the company, its financials,  
management, and the purpose of raising funds etc. The public offer aims to provide  
ownership and investment opportunities to a wide range of investors. Only a public  
company can issue public offer. Sections 23 to 41 under Part I of Chapter III of the Act  
are applicable to public companies for issue of its securities through prospectus i.e.,  
‘public offer’. A public offer includes initial public offer or further public offer of  
securities to the public by a company, or an offer for sale of securities to the public by an  
existing shareholder, through issue of a prospectus. In this process the company issues a  
prospectus.  
Private placement is a method of raising capital by offering shares or debentures to a  
select group of individuals or institutions, excluding the general public. This method is  
often used to raise funds from a limited number of investors, such as high net worth  
individuals, venture capitalists, or institutional investors. Section 42 of the Act provides  
that a company can make a private placement to a select group of persons or identified  
persons as identified by the Board of the company. A company making a private  
placement cannot offer its securities through any public advertisements or utilise any  
marketing, media, or distribution agents or channels to inform the public about such an  
offer. If the offer is advertised or marketed, it will be considered a public offer and not a  
private placement by the company.  
NOTE: Include the other important compliances for each of these methods. Refer to the  
Notes in the course.  
16  
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
Thus, we can say that a public offer involves offering shares or debentures to the general  
public through a prospectus, while private placement targets a select group of investors  
without the need for a prospectus. Both methods have specific rules and regulations to  
safeguard the interests of investors and ensure transparency in capital raising activities.

Question no. 10. What is prospectus and the various types of prospectuses? Explain in detail  
as per the Companies Act, 2013.  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
A prospectus is a formal document that provides essential information about a  
company to potential investors. It is a very important document used during public  
offer to communicate important details and facts about the company's financial status,  
operations, management, and the securities being offered. The primary purpose of a  
prospectus is to enable investors to make informed decisions before investing in  
the company's securities. It can be said that a prospectus is essentially an invitation to  
the public to invest in a company's securities. It contains comprehensive and accurate  
information that helps investors evaluate the company's financial position, future  
prospects, and risk factors associated with the investment. The Companies Act, 2013, and  
the Securities and Exchange Board of India regulations outline the specific requirements  
and disclosures that must be included in a prospectus. The prospectus plays a critical  
role in maintaining transparency, ensuring investor protection, and promoting fair  
practices in the capital markets.  
As per Companies Act, 2013 (“Act”) Section 2(70) “prospectus” means any document  
described or issued as a prospectus and includes a red herring prospectus referred to in  
section 32 or shelf prospectus referred to in section 31 or any notice, circular,  
advertisement or other document inviting offers from the public for the subscription or  
purchase of any securities of a body corporate. In other words, a prospectus is any  
advertisement, circular, or document that invites public to subscribe to any shares or  
debentures of a corporate body which is a public company. The company’s operations  
and objectives, along with the purpose of the securities being offered are disclosed in a  
17  
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
prospectus. A private company cannot issue a prospectus because private companies  
are relatively small in size, thus, they issue fewer shares, and share transferability is  
limited. A prospectus contains details such as name of the company, registered address,  
nature and capital structure, date of opening and closing of the issue etc.  
Section 26 deals with the legal requirements for the issuance of a prospectus as  
under:  
 prospectus must be issued by or on behalf of a public company;  
 make a declaration about the compliance of the provisions of the Copanies Act  
and a statement to the effect that nothing in the prospectus is contrary to the  
provisions of the Act, the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and the  
Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 and the rules and regulations  
made thereunder;  
 the date stated in the prospectus will be regarded to be the date of its issuance of  
a prospectus;  
 on or before the date of its publication, a copy of it has to be delivered to the  
Registrar for filing, signed by every person who is named therein as a director or  
proposed director of the company or by his duly authorised attorney;  
 a statement claiming to be made by an expert may not be included in a prospectus  
issued unless the expert is a person who is not, and has not been, involved in any  
form of management or operations of the company. Written consent to the issue  
of the prospectus must be given, and must not withdraw his consent prior to  
delivery of a copy of the prospectus to the Registrar for filing. A statement to that  
effect must also be included in the prospectus.  
 every prospectus issued must mention that a copy has been supplied to the  
Registrar for filing and must specify any documents that must be attached to the  
copy supplied;  
 a prospectus issued more than 90 days after a copy is delivered to the Registrar,  
is deemed to be invalid.  
 if a prospectus is issued in violation of provisions under Section 26, the company  
shall be penalized with a fine not less than fifty rupees and not exceeding three  
lakh rupees. Any individual who is knowingly a party to the issue of such  
prospectus shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand  
rupees but which may extend to three lakh rupees.  
According to the Companies Act, 2013, there are four types of prospectus: Red Herring,  
Shelf, Abridged, and Deemed.  
 Red Herring Prospectus: Section 32  



it is the initial version of the prospectus filed with the regulatory authority  
before the public issue of securities;  
does not provide detailed information about the quantum or the price of the  
securities being offered by the company;  
a company that intends to offer securities to the public can issue a red  
herring prospectus before issuing the original prospectus;  
18  
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  


it must be filed with the Registrar at least three days prior to the opening  
of the subscription list and offers;  
a red herring prospectus is subject to the same obligations as a prospectus,  
and any difference between the red herring prospectus and the prospectus  
must be identified as ‘deviations in the prospectus’.  

upon the closing of the offer of securities the prospectus must state the  
total capital raised, whether by debt or share capital, and the closing price  
of the securities, as well as any other details not included in the red herring  
prospectus and must be filed with the Registrar and the SEBI.  
 Shelf Prospectus: Section 31  



it is a type of prospectus that allows a company to offer multiple issues of  
securities over a specific period without filing a new prospectus each time;  
it provides flexibility to issuers to tap into the market as and when they  
require funding, subject to certain conditions;  
it is valid up to one year, during which the company can issue multiple  
offerings under the same document. The period of one year shall begin  
from the date of opening of the first offer of securities under the prospectus  
and in respect to subsequent offers of securities issued during the period  
of validity of that prospectus in accordance with the guidelines issued by  
SEBI. A fresh prospectus is not required to be issued for the offer of  
securities;  

a company filing a shelf prospectus must file an information memorandum  
with the Registrar prior to the issue of subsequent offer of securities,  
containing all updated charges in the facts, the company’s financial position  
that changed between the previous offer of securities and the succeeding  
offer of securities, or any other changes.  
 Deemed Prospectus: Section 25  

it refers to any document that offers securities to the public and contains all  
the information that a regular prospectus would include;  

it can be in various formats, such as an advertisement, a circular, or a  
notice however, if the contents of the document meets the criteria of a  
prospectus, it is treated as a deemed prospectus, and the company must  
follow the regulations applicable to a regular prospectus;  


it contains an offer for sale made by the intermediary or issuing house on  
behalf of a company that allots or agrees to allot its shares or securities  
through an intermediary. A company usually opts for a deemed prospectus  
to avoid complying with regulations issued by the SEBI;  
it is considered a document of offer for sale if it meets either of the following  
criterias:  
o the intermediary made an offer to sell shares to the public within six  
months of the allotment of shares; or  
19  
Companies Act-Descriptive Question Notes  
o the company which allotted its shares to the intermediary has not  
received payment in exchange for the shares the offer for sale was  
made by the intermediary.  
 Abridged Prospectus: Section 2(1)  


it is a summarized version of the full prospectus;  
it provides an overview of the key information investors need to know,  
including the objectives of the issue, financial information, management  
details, and the terms of the offering.  


as per the definition of in the Act “abridged prospectus” means a  
memorandum containing such salient features of a prospectus as may be  
specified by the Securities and Exchange Board by making regulations in  
this behalf;  
as per section 33 of the Act no form of application for the purchase of any  
of the securities of a company shall be issued unless such form is  
accompanied by an abridged prospectus. However, this shall not be  
applicable f it is shown that the form of application was issued:  
o in connection with a bona fide invitation to a person to enter into an  
underwriting agreement with respect to such securities; or in  
relation to securities which were not offered to the public.  
Liability for misstatement in a prospectus can be classified into civil liability under  
Section 35 and criminal liability under Section 34 of the Companies Act, 2013.  
A prospectus is thus, a comprehensive document that contains essential information about  
a company and its securities, designed to inform potential investors. Each prospectus  
performs differently, which may help a company to make a reasonable investment  
decision. Identifying the appropriate type of prospectus for issuing securities helps the  
company to make an informed investment strategy. As a result, a prospectus is essential  
for every public company.  
NOTE: For the liability elaborate the points as per the respective sections.
